He knew what those rolls did — had seen them work from the other side of a trial more times than he could count, watched survivors patch hook wounds and blade cuts in the middle of a chase and come back functional in minutes. The Fog's particular generosity with medical supplies had always struck him as one of its stranger qualities, that it would hand out tools that undermined the whole point of his job. But the point of the trial as a whole was fear, not damage, and fear didn't require permanent injury. He'd just never had occasion to use one himself. He picked it up. Looked across the yard. David met his eye for a hard moment before turning to go back to the others, busying himself with getting everyone stable and upright, swatting Orela away for the 20 th time in as many minutes. Danny looked at the bandage roll in his hand for a moment longer. Something complicated and uncomfortable settled into his chest, formless and unresolved, sitting alongside everything else the night had deposited there that he hadn't sorted through yet. He didn't have a name for it. Didn't particularly want to find one right now. He unwrapped the bandage and got to work. The difference was immediate — proper materials doing the job properly, the ache in his ribs dropping from a shout to a manageable complaint. He'd be sore for a while. But leagues better than before. The medkit died out too soon, as it always tended to do, but it was enough to get people functional. Walking-wounded functional, coughing-through-it functional, the usual grade of operational that the Fog seemed designed to maintain regardless of what the trial threw at people. It was always a little insane how well those kits worked. Tonight it felt more insane than usual. Nobody said it out loud — nobody had to. The trial didn't care what they'd been through. The gate wasn't opening without the work done, the campfire wasn't reachable without the gate, and standing in a flooded playground indefinitely wasn't an option anyone was willing to consider. So they went, in ones and twos, moving slower than usual but moving nonetheless, and finished what the night had interrupted. The last generator caught with a familiar surge, and the group moved together in an exhausted slog toward the gate as it ground open with the same shriek of rust and neglect it always made. The Fog met them at the threshold, and the first tendrils of it were an absolute blessing. The ache in bruised bones softening at the edges. The rawness in waterlogged lungs dulling toward something that might eventually become ordinary tired. The sharpest edges of the last several hours filing themselves down into something the mind could carry without bleeding. Danny trailed behind the group as they supported each other out of Bedham and towards the promise of a proper rest. Nobody had made a call for or against it. The logic had resolved itself somewhere in the yard while they were finishing the generators — he'd been there, he had nowhere else to be, and the group had collectively filed that under a problem for later and kept moving. He trailed a few feet behind David, water still dripping from his hair onto the gateway floor, and tried not to think too hard about what came next. The Entity’s barricades slammed up through the gate floor like knives, black and jagged, cleaving the path clean in half between Danny and the others. They howled as they emerged, shrieking metal and bone, driving a wedge between survivors and their tag-along. Everyone halted and turned back, the Fog briefly catching the shape of their surprise, as if the building and the water and the whole terrible night had temporarily made them forget what he was. Danny didn’t seem surprised. The gate had never been his. That was just the shape of things. It had always been a survivor’s exit — a path out of the trial and back to the fire. The best a killer could hope for, if they crossed it at all, was a return to their personal domain. And Danny didn't have one. He'd come into the Fog without a home — that was just the fact of it. No domain waiting for him, no personal architecture to return to between trials. He'd made do. He drifted. Crashed with others. Slept in corners of Myers’ neighborhood when no one noticed. Used houses that had long since lost their original owners. It was a comfortable life, floating untethered from domain to domain, as if the entirety of the Entity’s realm itself had been his home. He'd never been to their campfire. None of his kind had. That door had never been open to him and he hadn't expected it to be. Danny met David’s gaze through the barricade, gave a tight nod he hoped was reassuring, and motioned for him to go on without him. He stood on his side of the barricade and looked at Danny through the gaps in the spikes with that same unreadable expression from across the yard. For a moment he looked almost like he might come back to the barrier, eyes glancing over the spikes as if there was something to be done about them, before the tension dropped from his shoulders and he sighed lightly. He gave a single nod. Small. The particular weight of it landing somewhere between acknowledgement and something Danny didn't have a clean name for. Then he turned and rejoined the group, and the Fog took them, and the gateway sat empty with its spikes still up. Danny stood at the barrier for a while.
